Intermittent fasting is widely discussed as a potential anti-aging strategy, but current evidence presents conflicting outcomes. One review highlights animal studies where intermittent fasting increased lifespans and slowed aging processes [d1], while multiple high‑credibility mouse studies using comprehensive aging measures found only limited or no anti‑aging effects [d2,d4,d6,d7]. Additional sources emphasize lifespan extension across model organisms without directly demonstrating slowed aging [d3], and popular‑press summaries echo the lack of concrete evidence in humans [d9].

Given these divergent findings, the exact extent to which intermittent fasting slows human aging remains unsettled based on the retrieved evidence. Some sources suggest plausible mechanisms like metabolic switching and autophagy [d1,d8], but others argue these do not translate into measurable slowing of aging when assessed across multiple physiological systems [d2,d4,d5,d6,d7].
